versionMessage: Ground in official Iceberg docs and operator blogs: maintenance order, compaction strategies, further reading
body:
Bottom line — Iceberg gives you an excellent table format, not an automatic maintenance crew. Cryo scans 13,236 tables, grades health A–F, admits work only when ROI and engine load allow, and routes rewrites to native fast-path or Spark/Trino. The incident that opens this page — 1,344 delete files on one scan — is what happens when nobody is watching.

One evening, a table called lms.silver_adminactions quietly grew to 1,344 position-delete files. Nobody had touched it. No alert had fired. Then a routine Spark read against it started throwing ConnectionPoolTimeoutException: Timeout waiting for connection from pool — not from a compaction job, but from Iceberg's own delete-loader, spinning up its own internal thread pool just to stitch 1,344 delete files back together on a single scan.

That's not a story about one broken table. It's a story about what Apache Iceberg doesn't do for you.

PASTE IMAGE · cryo-hero-iceberg-rot.png
From docs/assets/confluence/cryo-maintenance-crew/. Day 0 vs Day 90 without maintenance — the same table quietly turns from a few clean files into metadata rot and delete-file overload.

The stakes: one table's rot, multiplied by 13,236

We run 13,236 tables on a single EKS cluster, fed by dozens of BigQuery-sourced pipelines — pw_medharthi_bq, curiousjr_bq, xylem_bq, neet_pg_bq, gyaane_bq, and more. If one delete-heavy table can quietly exhaust a connection pool before anyone notices, multiply that risk by 13,236, and multiply the manual toil of catching each one by however many engineers we can spare in a given week.

That's not a maintenance plan — it's an incident queue with a delay timer.

PASTE IMAGE · chart-fleet-scale.png
From docs/assets/confluence/cryo-maintenance-crew/. One EKS cluster, 13,236 Iceberg tables — the multiplier behind every quiet rot story.

What Iceberg actually gives you (and what it doesn't)

Iceberg's table format is genuinely excellent: hidden partitioning, snapshot isolation, schema evolution, time travel, engine-agnostic metadata — the guarantees Netflix originally wanted when moving off Hive-style directory tables (Tabular on Iceberg in modern architecture). What it doesn't give you is any promise that those things stay fast. Iceberg hands you a beautifully organized filing cabinet and leaves the filing to you.

Four things rot if nobody intervenes:

  • Small files pile up. Frequent or streaming writes create many tiny data files. Every additional file is another open/seek/plan cost at query time — read performance degrades quietly, file by file. Production guidance typically targets 256–512 MB Parquet files after compaction (Dremio on the small-files problem).

  • Delete files accumulate. Merge-on-read tables don't rewrite on update or delete — they append delete markers. Every scan has to merge those markers back against the data files. Left alone, this is exactly what took down our connection pool: 1,344 delete files, one query. See merge-on-read and delete-file overhead at read time for why this scales badly.

  • Snapshot history grows unbounded. No expiry means metadata (metadata.json, manifest lists) grows forever, planning gets slower, and storage cost climbs from data files nobody can see anymore but Iceberg still has to retain. expire_snapshots removes snapshot metadata — reclaiming storage still needs orphan cleanup (RisingWave on snapshot expiration vs GC).

  • Physical layout never matches the query pattern. Iceberg writes data in whatever order it arrives. If a table is partitioned by day but queried by month, or sorted by nothing when most filters hit one column, every scan reads far more data than it needs to — and nothing in the format itself will ever tell you that.

We felt the fourth one directly: a table's health score dropped 20 points for exactly this reason — daily partitioning on a table actually queried by month, plus a small-file fragmentation check that, we later found, didn't even account for tables with a single, perfectly-compacted file. Health scoring itself needed maintenance.

A table left alone doesn't fail loudly. It fails as a slow, compounding tax that eventually shows up as someone else's incident.

The maintenance playbook — documented everywhere, automated nowhere by default

Iceberg ships four maintenance primitives. The official maintenance guide and every serious operator blog agree on what they are — and on the fact that nothing in the format schedules or prioritizes them for you (IOMETE: what Iceberg ships vs what teams still build).

OperationSpark procedure (typical)What it fixes
Expire snapshotsexpire_snapshotsOld snapshot metadata; dereferences data files only held by expired snapshots
Remove orphan filesremove_orphan_filesPhysical files in storage with no live metadata reference (failed writes, aborted jobs)
Compact / optimizerewrite_data_filesSmall files, delete-file accumulation, layout (binpack / sort / z-order)
Rewrite manifestsrewrite_manifestsFragmented manifest metadata after heavy compaction

Order matters. Run expire_snapshots before remove_orphan_files. Expiration converts snapshot-pinned files into orphan-eligible files; cleaning orphans first misses the largest reclaimable storage category (LakeOps orphan cleanup, automating maintenance sequences). Cryo's Planner preserves this order: expire → remove orphans → optimize → optimize manifests.

flowchart LR
    A[expire_snapshots] --> B[remove_orphan_files]
    B --> C[optimize / rewrite_data_files]
    C --> D[rewrite_manifests]
    A -.->|"dereferences old data files"| B
    B -.->|"reclaims S3 bytes"| C
    C -.->|"fewer files, applied deletes"| D

Compaction strategies — same primitives, very different cost

Compaction is not one operation. Teams pick a strategy based on write pattern, query filters, and how much compute they can spend (Dremio compaction guide, BigData Boutique best practices).

StrategyWhat it doesWhen it fitsCompute
BinpackMerges small files to target size; reconciles deletesStreaming tables, tight maintenance windows, MoR cleanupLowest
SortClusters data by chosen columns while compactingPredictable filters on 1–2 columns (e.g. user_id, event_date)Medium
Z-orderMulti-column clustering for multidimensional filtersAnalytics with several common filter dimensionsHigher

Cryo routes binpack-style compaction through the native fast path when possible; sort and z-order rewrites go to Spark/Trino. Smart Maintenance recommends layout changes from query telemetry — but a human approves before any physical rewrite runs.

Industry pattern: production lakehouses see "slow drift" — small files accumulate, manifests grow, snapshots pile up, delete files compound — "nothing is broken, but everything costs more than it should" (survey of nine maintenance approaches). That is the wound Cryo is aimed at.

Why not cron jobs? Why not just buy a managed platform?

Both are reasonable first instincts, and we tried the first one before building Cryo.

Raw Spark procedures — rewrite_data_files, expire_snapshots, remove_orphan_files — are the right primitives. But a cron job that fires OPTIMIZE on a schedule has no idea whether a given rewrite is worth its own compute cost, no way to avoid admitting too much work onto a shared cluster at once, and no concept of "this table's retain_last setting is protecting all four of its snapshots regardless of age" — a bug we hit and fixed on a real table this quarter. Cron jobs execute; they don't decide. That's the same gap every DIY Airflow-plus-dbt setup runs into — an Airflow DAG that scans, a second DAG that decides, a pile of dbt macros carrying the actual maintenance logic, and none of it sharing state or exposing a UI.

Every managed option is genuinely good — if you've already committed to that vendor's compute and table format. AWS Glue Table Optimizers run compaction, snapshot retention, and orphan deletion as managed background jobs for Glue-cataloged tables (AWS Glue storage optimization). Starburst and Dremio wrap the same SQL procedures with scheduling (Starburst automated maintenance). They solve "run maintenance" — not always "decide which 13,236 tables deserve compute today under live Trino load."

We hadn't committed to renting the whole warehouse. We wanted maintenance intelligence without telemetry leaving our infra (SaaS control planes like LakeOps send query telemetry externally) and without losing multi-engine routing — native fast path plus Spark/Trino when MoR deletes or Hive catalogs demand it.

Decision: Cryo

Cryo is a self-hosted Iceberg maintenance platform: it continuously scans tables, scores their health, decides — with a real cost/benefit model, not a fixed schedule — what's worth fixing, and routes the actual rewrite to whichever engine can do it fastest.

Iceberg transforms our data lake into an orderly library — Cryo is the crew that keeps re-shelving it as new books keep arriving.

Features, bucket by bucket

Three groups, mirroring how the platform is actually organized internally.

Maintenance

  • Sources & Destinations — discover from REST/Hive/Glue; maintain on whichever engine the preset targets.

  • Planner — engine-agnostic chunks with GB budgets, partition caps, cooldowns, off-peak windows.

  • Governor — load-aware admission, per-replica caps, round-robin across destinations.

  • Presets — operations + params + engine + schedule + selection rules in one profile.

  • Assignment UX — filter fleet by grade, size, drift; bulk assign presets.

Health & observability

  • Scanner — A–F grades, compaction priority, S3 cost estimate.

  • Dashboards — fleet health, audit timeline, live run console.

  • Anomaly detection — drift on null-rate, size, file-count, small-file ratio.

  • Cost & inventory — opt-in S3/CUR ingestion for real spend numbers.

  • Owner alerting — SLA breaches notify owners and subscribers.

PASTE IMAGE · cryo-health-grades-dashboard.png
From docs/assets/confluence/cryo-maintenance-crew/. Fleet health at a glance — letter grades, small-file %, delete ratio, and snapshot age on every table.

The mechanics of a single rewrite

sequenceDiagram
    participant T as Iceberg table
    participant S as Scanner
    participant G as Governor
    participant V as Plan Verifier
    participant E as Engine (native or Spark/Trino)

    T->>S: metadata scan (no live $files on hot path)
    S->>G: health grade + compaction candidate
    G->>G: ROI gate + live engine load check
    alt admitted
        G->>V: rendered plan vs live catalog
        V->>E: dispatch rewrite
        E->>T: fewer files, fresher snapshots, better layout
    else refused
        G-->>G: log refusal (QPP / load / ROI)
    end

PASTE IMAGE · chart-health-deductions.png
From docs/assets/confluence/cryo-maintenance-crew/. Health scoring is itemized — partition mismatch and delete ratio can cost 20 points each, not one opaque grade.

  • Scanner: walks every table's metadata and computes a health score — small-file fragmentation, delete-file ratio, partition-to-query fit, snapshot age — and itemizes exactly which deduction cost how many points, not just a single opaque grade.

  • Governor: the admission control layer. Before any rewrite runs, it checks a ROI gate (is the expected benefit — latency, storage, request cost — worth the compute cost of rewriting?) and admits work in waves, round-robin across destinations, so one noisy table can't starve the rest of the fleet.

  • Plan Verifier: statically checks a rendered maintenance plan against the live catalog before it's ever enqueued — a proof-carrying check, not a hope-it-works dispatch.

  • Native fast-path engine: talks directly to S3 and the Iceberg REST catalog for straightforward compaction and snapshot expiry — no JVM, minutes not hours.

  • Spark / Trino engine: the fallback for what the fast path can't safely do — delete-heavy merge-on-read tables, Hive Metastore-backed sources, and custom sort/z-order rewrites that need a real query engine underneath them.

  • Smart Maintenance: reads real query telemetry per table — which columns get filtered, how often, how selectively — and recommends a sort or z-order strategy instead of guessing. Nothing executes without a human approving it first.

Analogy: the Governor works like airport ground control, not a single gate agent — it doesn't just check one flight's paperwork, it watches total runway load and boards planes in controlled waves so nobody stalls the whole airport. The ROI gate is closer to a renovation contractor who won't start a $10,000 kitchen remodel that will only add $2,000 to the house's value — it says no to work that doesn't pay for itself, even work it's fully capable of doing.

AI scope — where it's real, and where it's still charts waiting for data

"AI" at Cryo isn't a chatbot bolted onto a dashboard. It's a handful of narrow, purpose-built components, most of them classic optimization or statistical models rather than LLM calls — plus one place where an LLM genuinely earns its keep: turning evidence into a plain-language explanation a human can act on.

ComponentWhat it actually isHuman in the loop?
Query Performance Prediction (QPP)Variance-aware p95 risk model; Governor refuses admission when predicted blow-upAutomated refusal
Plan VerifierStatic proof-carrying check against live catalogAuto-block unsafe plans
Layout recommendationsCost-based sort/z-order from query telemetry (WAIR-style)Pending until approved
Union searchpgvector over metadata for unionable tablesSearch-assist
Anomaly briefsLLM explains scan + query-pattern evidenceExplanation only
SkillsetsVersioned prompt + tool bundles with outcome trackingGovernance layer

Honest caveat: advanced / AI / FinOps / anomaly surfaces are partially implemented and only become useful once query-log telemetry ingestion is switched on. Until a fleet opts into that, expect empty charts on those pages — not broken ones. This is a rollout gap, not a code gap.

Research grounding

Cryo's features aren't invented from scratch. Several map directly to recent papers, with a working test exercising the core logic of each.

PaperFeature
AutoComp (SIGMOD 2025, LinkedIn — paper)Multi-objective compaction at 100K+ tables: rank by benefit vs compute cost; top-K under budget — same problem shape as Cryo's Governor ROI gate
Proof-Carrying AI AgentsPlan Verifier — statically checks a plan against the live catalog before enqueue
EasyTUSEmbedding-based unionable-table search across the fleet
Observation Lakehouse (SANER 2026)Append-only archive of every actuation, for audit and replay
Zero-Scan Data Quality (FORMATS '26)Per-column null rates, value bounds, and drift from manifest metadata — no data scans required
Variance-aware QPP (CLOUD 2026)Query performance prediction — the Governor refuses jobs predicted to blow p95
PTO (IBM Research, SIGMOD/PACMMOD 2026)Joint partition/sort/file-size optimization — 11–36% avg latency reduction reported on TPC workloads
WAIR (arXiv 2602.23289, 2026)Workload-aware incremental reclustering — closest match to Smart Maintenance layout scoring

PTO's full text sits behind the ACM Digital Library paywall — we verified abstract and reported numbers, not algorithm internals.

The honest version: Cryo doesn't make Iceberg maintenance disappear. It makes it something a health score decides instead of something a person has to remember.

Cost projections

Cryo's Scanner already computes a real per-table S3 cost estimate as part of every health grade — this isn't a section where we invent a company-wide savings number. It's a walkthrough of the shape of that model, so the estimate a table actually gets isn't a black box.

Cost driverWhat changesIllustrative example
Storage reclaimedexpire_snapshots + orphan cleanup~400 GB unreferenced snapshots freed on one neglected table
Request costFewer, larger files per scan10,000 files → ~500 ≈ 95% fewer object reads per scan

OSS today, and a real SaaS option tomorrow

Cryo is Apache-2.0 licensed today — genuinely open, not source-available-with-an-asterisk. Any team can read the planner, audit the Governor's admission logic, and self-host without a vendor relationship.

  • OSS core stays the core: scanner, planner, governor, engines, presets, and the UI.

  • Managed control plane could remove painful self-host ops (Postgres, Redis, K8s) for teams that want the dashboard without operating the stack.

  • Enterprise governance — SSO, audit retention, multi-tenant isolation by default — is the gap the honest "who this isn't for yet" list already names.

Strategic option, not roadmap commitment. Multi-tenant SaaS isn't supported today by design — tenant isolation is opt-in, not default.

Trade-offs — what's still open

Sort/z-order execution is deliberately not autonomous: a recommendation sits in pending until a human approves it. A physical rewrite of a production table is resource-consuming and semi-reversible — we'd rather have a human in the loop than a system quietly reshuffling 13,236 tables on its own judgment.

The Spark/Trino fallback path is slower and costlier than the native fast path by design. The ROI gate still runs in shadow mode for some destinations while we build confidence in its cost model. Launch-tier surface (scanner, health grading, planner, governor, engines, presets, audit log, auth) is real and tested; advanced AI/FinOps/anomaly tiers are honestly labeled partial until telemetry adoption catches up.

Where this leaves us

None of this makes Iceberg maintenance solved — it makes it observable, prioritized, and mostly automatic, which is a very different thing from either "someone remembers to run a script" or "a vendor's black box decides for us." We've already caught real bugs this way: a retain_last setting silently protecting every snapshot on a low-snapshot-count table, a hardcoded catalog name breaking cross-catalog dispatch, a connection pool sized for a world without 1,344-delete-file tables.

The wound that opened this page is closed. The next one is probably already growing on some table we haven't scanned yet — which is exactly why Cryo runs continuously instead of when someone remembers to check.

Questions, pushback, or a table you think is quietly rotting? Come find us.
